Whittier 360 predicts six California propositions will pass, six will fail; two remain too close to call
Rebecca Canales (https://www.whittier360newsnetwork.com/profile/f8c940d8-e5eb-46fd-8a58-6834773d6406/profile)
5 minutes ago
5 min read
ELECTION FORECAST
Caption: Whittier 360 News Network forecasts six California propositions will pass and six will fail in the November 3, 2026 election, with two too close to call. AI-generated editorial illustration; predictions are not election results.
Whittier 360 News Network predicts that California voters will approve six statewide propositions and reject six others in the November 3 election. Two additional measures remain too close to call.
These predictions are part of an experimental forecasting approach that Whittier 360 is testing. After the election, we will compare our forecasts with certified results to assess their accuracy.
The predictions below are not endorsements or recommendations on how to vote. A forecast of passage does not indicate our support for a measure, and a forecast of defeat does not indicate our opposition.
Here are our predictions for all 14 statewide propositions, presented in numerical order, with explanations of what each would do if approved.
Proposition 1 — Housing affordability bonds
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for affordable housing programs. Funding would support rental housing, veterans’ mortgages, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable homes and down-payment assistance.
The state estimates repayment costs of approximately $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years.
Proposition 2 — State budget reserves
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 2 would change California’s rules for building its rainy day fund and making additional payments toward state debts. The changes would increase state budget reserves and continue extra debt payments for a longer period.
The reserve fund helps the state manage economic downturns and fluctuations in revenue.
Proposition 3 — Permanent extension of higher income taxes
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 3 would make permanent an existing income tax increase on high-income earners that otherwise expires in 2031. The official summary identifies an individual income threshold above $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation.
The measure would preserve an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue by continuing those tax rates, with revenues allocated to public education.
Proposition 4 — Public financing of election campaigns
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 4 would repeal the prohibition that prevents the state and most local governments from establishing publicly funded campaign programs.
It would allow qualifying programs rather than automatically provide public money to every candidate. Programs would face restrictions on eligible recipients and spending, and could not use money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety.
Proposition 5 — Changes to recall elections
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 5 would change how vacancies are filled after successful recalls. Voters would no longer choose a replacement candidate on the same ballot used to decide whether to remove an official.
Instead, vacancies would generally be filled through a later special election or an appointment, depending on the office and timing. The measure would preserve the ability to recall officials while changing the replacement process.
Proposition 37 — Homebuying assistance
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 37 would create a homebuying assistance program financed through up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. Eligible buyers could obtain fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of the purchase price of qualifying newly constructed homes priced below approximately $1.5 million.
Buyers would have to meet income and residency requirements, occupy the home and contribute at least a 3% down payment. Homeowners’ loan payments would repay the bonds.
Proposition 38 — Medical research bonds
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half would go to a University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and half to research grants.
Estimated repayment costs are $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years. Revenue generated by the research could offset some or all of those costs, but that outcome is not guaranteed.
Proposition 39 — Additional voter identification requirements
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 39 would require government-issued identification for in-person voting. Mail voters would have to place the last four digits of their designated government-issued identification number on their ballot envelope, matching their registration information.
The measure also would require citizenship-verification efforts, annual reporting and free state-issued voter identification cards upon request. Estimated implementation costs range from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually.
Proposition 40 — One-time billionaire wealth tax
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time tax equal to 5% of the wealth of covered taxpayers with assets exceeding $1 billion. Revenue would primarily support health care.
The state estimates a temporary revenue increase totaling tens of billions of dollars over several years, alongside a possible ongoing reduction in income tax revenue from billionaires.
Proposition 41 — Tax audits and state spending limits
Whittier 360 forecast: TOO CLOSE TO CALL
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exclude their revenues from California’s constitutional spending limit. It also would require pre-election reviews of programs slated to receive funding from voter-proposed special taxes and recurring audits of programs supported by new special taxes.
The proposal could affect other tax measures on the same ballot through provisions addressing conflicting measures. Whittier 360 is withholding a pass-or-fail prediction.
Proposition 42 — Restrictions on new property and retroactive taxes
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on ownership of personal property, including financial assets and business interests. Personal property in this context means property other than real estate.
It also would restrict certain retroactive taxes and apply to new taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026. The measure contains provisions addressing conflicts with other propositions approved on the same ballot.
Proposition 43 — Higher approval threshold for local special taxes
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 43 would require two-thirds voter approval for voter-proposed local special taxes, replacing the current simple-majority threshold for those measures beginning January 1, 2027.
Special taxes raise money for specified purposes. The change could make it harder to approve certain local funding proposals and could reduce future growth in local tax revenue.
Proposition 44 — Community health clinic spending requirements
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 44 would require certain nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on qualifying program services advancing their charitable purpose.
Covered clinics failing to meet the requirement could face penalties. The proposal would create new state oversight responsibilities, with administrative costs funded through fees.
Proposition 45 — Environmental review changes
Whittier 360 forecast: TOO CLOSE TO CALL
Proposition 45 would change California Environmental Quality Act procedures for qualifying projects, including many housing, transportation, water and health projects.
It would tighten deadlines for environmental review and court challenges and limit the scope of certain judicial reviews. Whittier 360 is withholding a pass-or-fail prediction because we consider the outcome too uncertain to call.
How the forecast will be evaluated
Our forecast contains six predictions of passage, six predictions of defeat and two uncalled contests. “Too close to call” means we are not predicting a winner; it does not mean we expect an exact tie.
We will assess the 12 pass-or-fail predictions against certified election results and report how many proved correct. The two uncalled measures will be identified separately rather than counted as successful predictions.
Voters will determine the outcomes. These forecasts represent Whittier 360’s assessment before the results are known.

REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

The forecast's 57.2% chance to pass looks high next to a polling average of 45.9%, so I want to see what model is behind it. I'm also recalling that similar ballot measures, like Props 15 and 89, failed, so I'll check whether the results are already in.

I'm questioning the onpointpolitics forecast, since its "History and structure" prior of 74.1% yes looks far too high next to California's record on public financing measures, where Prop 89 in 2006 got about 26% and Prop 15 in 2010 about 43%. The model then blends that prior with a 45.9% polling average to reach 51.1%, which makes me suspect the prior is built on legislatively referred statutes in California

I'm noting that the forecast's prior seems to assume public financing measures pass the way other statutes do, which the historical results contradict. I'm also thinking the date is around November 2, 2026 or later, so I'll look for actual results on the Prop 4 public financing ban.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.

Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

ry for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
July 6, 2026
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. I'm checking the PPIC October numbers for Prop 4: 45% yes, 52% no, with support below a majority in every region except the Bay Area at 51%. That points toward the measure failing. Still, I want to test that against PPIC's track record on ballot measures, looking at cases where a sub-50% reading still ended in passage.

Now I'm going through PPIC's past results on 2024 propositions, to check how their October numbers compared with the final votes.

I'm now weighing the Berkeley IGS poll, which shows 41-41 with 18% undecided, and I think undecided voters will likely break toward no, so the outcome probably lands around 45-55. I'm also factoring in the 2026 environment, where Democratic enthusiasm looks high in a midterm with Trump as president, and I'm still working through how that shifts the picture.

I'm working through the Democratic share of likely voters to estimate the overall yes vote, which comes out to roughly 46%. I'm also noting that the No side has almost no money behind it while Yes has only about $1M, so in a low-information race the ballot label itself may be doing most of the persuading.

I'm checking whether the election results are already in, since the question might be asked after November 3, 2026, so I'm looking for news from November 4 onward.

I'm searching for any reports on California proposition results, checking for coverage dated November 4, 2026 or later.

Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason)

Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40 in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. | Jae C. Hong/AP
DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.
GOOD MORNING. Happy Wednesday. Thanks for waking up with California Playbook.
Like what you’re reading? Sign up (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/californiaplaybook) to get California Playbook in your inbox, and forward it to a friend. Have a tip for Playbook? Or you can text us at ‪ 916-562-0685 ‬‪ — save it as “ CA Playbook ” in your contacts.
WHO WON THE DAY? Prop 40 opponents , who received good news in the PPIC poll.
WHERE’S GAVIN? In Los Angeles, having a fireside chat with California Science Center CEO Jeffrey Rudolph during a media preview of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.
Read the full story from Christine Mui and Sean McMinn here (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/billionaires-spending-california-wealth-tax-01137778) .
IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.

Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. Meet the Berkeley IGS Poll Director
Read Mark DiCamillo's bio here. (https://igs.berkeley.edu/people/mark-dicamillo)
The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).
IGS Poll (2016 - current) and California Field Poll data (1950's to 2015) can be downloaded from UC Berkeley Dataverse (https://datasets.lib.berkeley.edu/dataverse/igs).

California billionaires tax trails in another poll days before election
The Berkeley IGS survey finds 50% oppose Proposition 40 and 42% support it. Two measures aimed at blocking the tax also lack majority support.

By John Woolfolk (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/john-woolfolk/) | jwoolfolk@bayareanewsgroup.com (mailto:jwoolfolk@bayareanewsgroup.com) | Bay Area News Group
PUBLISHED: October 29, 2026 at 12:25 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 30, 2026 at 4:46 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

Amid wealthy opponents’ ad blitz, Prop. 40 is losing ground (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/)
“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

Proposition 4 : Allow public funding of election campaigns
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 4 would lift the state ban on using public money to pay for candidates' campaigns, so state and local governments could create public campaign financing programs if they chose. It does not create any program itself. It sets broad rules: money meant for education, transportation or public safety can't be used, candidates must show broad support and accept spending limits, and public funds can't pay legal fees, fines or repay a candidate's own loans.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 4
What it does Lets the state, counties, general law cities and districts create public campaign financing programs. Creates no program
State cost A few hundred thousand dollars a year for the FPPC (Legislative Analyst)
City of LA's own program In place since 1993; $11.08 million in matching funds paid to 2026 City candidates as of Sept. 30
Vote needed Simple majority
Money raised, Jan. 1 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $756,541.89 (one committee). Against: no committee
Outside spending Against: $55,363.68, mostly Reform California's (shared with other props). For: $43,211.14
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 45% yes, 52% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 41% yes, 41% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database and the City Ethics Commission.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , What would change , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 4 mean?
State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
What does a no vote on Proposition 4 mean?
State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
What would Proposition 4 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates state costs of a few hundred thousand dollars a year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public financing programs. The cost of any actual program would depend on which governments create one and how.
What it means for the City of LA
Los Angeles already runs a public matching funds program for City candidates, allowed because the current ban does not reach charter cities. Proposition 4 would not create, fund or end that program. It would let Los Angeles County, LAUSD and other local governments create programs. Proposition 4 also writes new rules for public financing programs. Neither the Legislative Analyst nor the City has said whether those rules would bind a charter city's own elections.
The details
Official title Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
Type Legislative statute amending the Political Reform Act, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SB 42, Chapter 245, Statutes of 2025)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. The Political Reform Act is a voter-approved initiative statute; the State Constitution (Article II, Section 10) lets the Legislature amend it only by a statute "approved by the electors," and provides that such measures take effect when "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
This is not the Proposition 4 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the bond for water, wildfire and climate projects, which passed with 59.8% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 4 passes
Public money for campaigns Banned for state offices and most local offices. The ban does not apply to city elections in certain charter cities; the Analyst names Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland and Berkeley as current examples that fund campaigns (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)) The ban is lifted. The state and any local government may create a program, but none is created by the measure (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm))
Which money can be used Not applicable Public funds “earmarked by any state or local entity for education, transportation, or public safety” cannot be used (text, Sec. 85300(a) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Who can get public money Not applicable Candidates who accept spending limits and meet “strict criteria” showing broad support in their district, such as a set number of small contributions or vouchers from residents. A law may not require more than $10 from each counted contributor, or a set number of signatures (text, Sec. 85300(b), (e)(7) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Spending limits Not applicable Programs may raise a participant’s limit, capped by a formula based on opponents’ money and outside spending (text, Sec. 85300(f) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Uses barred Not applicable No public funds for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate’s own loans. A candidate who takes public funds may never repay their own campaign loan from any source (text, Sec. 85300(c)-(d) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Fairness rule Not applicable Programs may not favor a party, incumbents or challengers (text, Sec. 85300(g) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Who runs local programs Not applicable Each local government. The state FPPC is not responsible for running or enforcing them, but would answer questions (text, Sec. 85300(h) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm))
Illegal foreign money Fine equal to the amount contributed or spent Fine of up to three times that amount (text, Sec. 85320(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3))
Later changes. The Legislature could change the definitions, the spending-limit formula and the FPPC’s role by a two-thirds vote with the Governor’s signature. Changing the other rules would need another vote of the people (text, Sec. 85300(i) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=3); Gov. Code sec. 81012 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=81012.)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
The City already has a program. Los Angeles voters created the City’s public matching funds program. It has been used in every City election since 1993 (City Ethics, 2019 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/news/access-to-public-matching-funds-significantly-increased-for-city-candidates/); City Ethics 2026 FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)). It is allowed today because the state ban does not apply to charter cities. The state Supreme Court ruled that in Johnson v. Bradley (1992), according to the Assembly Elections Committee’s analysis of SB 42 (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
How the City program works in 2026 (City Ethics 2026 FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)):
The City pays $6 for each $1 of a qualified contribution from an individual, up to $143 per contributor for Council and $257 for citywide offices.
To qualify, a candidate must get at least $5 each from 100 residents of the district or City, raise a minimum total from City residents ($14,300 for Council, $38,600 for City Attorney or Controller, $77,100 for Mayor), accept spending limits, cap their own money, face an opponent on the ballot, and debate or hold a town hall.
Maximum payments per candidate: $189,000 in a Council primary and $236,000 in a Council general election; $1,257,000 and $1,507,000 for Mayor.
The money comes from a City trust fund that the Charter requires the Council to fund each year, from City revenue only (City Charter sec. 471 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/wp-content/uploads/Laws-Campaigns-Matching-Funds-Charter-471.pdf)). The proposed 2026-27 budget puts $4,275,471 from the General Fund into the Matching Campaign Funds Trust Fund. The 2025-26 adopted budget shows no appropriation, after $4,075,427 in 2024-25 (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget, p. 372 (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=372)).
In the 2026 City elections , the City Ethics Commission’s totals page showed $11,076,890.66 in matching funds paid as of Sept. 30: $7,460,256.62 for the primary and $3,616,634.04 for the general election (City Ethics election totals (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)).
What Proposition 4 would and would not do to it.
Proposition 4 does not create, fund, cap or repeal the City’s program (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
It would let governments that now fall under the ban, such as Los Angeles County, LAUSD and the Community College District, create their own programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm); Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5)). None would have to.
Proposition 4 rewrites the state law (Government Code Section 85300) with new conditions for any public financing program. The Legislative Analyst does not say whether those conditions would apply to a charter city’s own elections, and the Assembly committee analysis does not address it (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm); Assembly Elections Committee analysis (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf)). We found no statement from the City Ethics Commission, City Attorney or City Council on Proposition 4 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
The Political Reform Act of 1974 is a voter-approved initiative statute, so the Legislature can amend it only by a two-thirds vote to further its purposes, or by a statute voters approve (Gov. Code sec. 81012 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=81012.)). SB 42 takes the second route: its text says it is submitted to the people under Article II, Section 10 of the Constitution (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)).
Dec. 5, 2024: SB 42 was introduced. Its lead authors are Sens. Tom Umberg, Ben Allen and Cervantes; the principal coauthors include Assemblymembers Berman, Kalra, Lee and Pellerin (SB 42 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
June 2, 2025: The Senate passed it 28-10 (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
July 2, 2025: The Assembly Elections Committee approved it 5-2. Its analysis lists the California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause and League of Women Voters of California as co-sponsors, and the California Taxpayers Association as the only registered opponent (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42); Assembly Elections Committee analysis, pp. 7-9 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=7)).
Sept. 12-13, 2025: The Assembly passed it 59-20 and the Senate agreed 29-8 (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Oct. 2, 2025: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it; it became Chapter 245, Statutes of 2025 (SB 42 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. Article II, Section 10 of the State Constitution provides that the Legislature “may amend or repeal an initiative statute by another statute that becomes effective only when approved by the electors,” and that an initiative statute or referendum “approved by a majority of votes cast thereon takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. II, sec. 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II)). The Political Reform Act says it may be amended “by a statute that becomes effective only when approved by the electors” (Gov. Code sec. 81012(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=81012.)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 73 (1988) created the ban (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101308/prop-4-allows-cities-to-create-public-campaign-financing-programs); Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)).
Voters rejected three earlier measures that would have lifted the ban and set up state programs: Proposition 25 (2000, 34.7% yes), Proposition 89 (2006, 25.7%) and Proposition 15 (2010, 42.7%) (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, p. 5 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=5)).
City of Los Angeles: the Charter’s matching funds section was last amended by Charter Amendment H, approved March 8, 2011 (Charter sec. 471 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/wp-content/uploads/Laws-Campaigns-Matching-Funds-Charter-471.pdf)). In 2019 the Council lowered the qualifying thresholds on the Ethics Commission’s recommendation (City Ethics, July 30, 2019 (https://ethics.lacity.gov/news/access-to-public-matching-funds-significantly-increased-for-city-candidates/)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument in favor, signed by Lorrel Plimier of the League of Women Voters of California, Catherine Kennedy of the California Nurses Association and Sen. Tom Umberg (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
“Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone.”
Similar systems work in “fourteen states and 26 localities.”
A local program costs “as little as $1 per resident each year.”
It “triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions.”
Their rebuttal, signed by Carmen Balber of Consumer Watchdog, Camerina Davidson of California NOW and Darius Kemp of California Common Cause, says California “is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns” (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, former FPPC commissioner Colleen McAndrews and Julian Canete of the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
There is “NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get.”
“Strict criteria” are left to “the same politicians who want to get your taxpayer money.”
Candidates could take public funds and special-interest money at the same time.
Outside the guide.
Jenny Farrell of the League of Women Voters of California told KQED that after Los Angeles adopted public financing, “14 or 15 of the members were elected using matching funds,” and the Council became majority women and people of color (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101308/prop-4-allows-cities-to-create-public-campaign-financing-programs)).
David Klein of the California Taxpayers Association told KQED that tax dollars should not go “to a candidate to then put out a hit piece mailer on an opponent” (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101308/prop-4-allows-cities-to-create-public-campaign-financing-programs)).
The Daily News editorial board wrote: “If charter cities want to keep experimenting, fine, that’s already allowed” (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What the records show
No limit on how much public money a candidate can get No campaign The measure sets no dollar cap; each program would set its own. It does require spending limits and caps how far a limit may be raised (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop4-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)). The City of LA’s program, for example, caps payments at $189,000 per Council primary candidate (City Ethics FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)).
No details on “strict criteria” No campaign The text requires criteria showing “broad-based support in their district” and bars requiring more than $1

In Los Angeles, participants may take private contributions under City limits (City Ethics FAQ (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/)).
It spends no tax dollars by itself Yes campaign The Analyst says it “does not create a public campaign finance system” and that state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars a year for FPPC advice (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/analysis.htm)).
As little as $1 per resident a year Yes campaign Not addressed by the Analyst. For Los Angeles, the proposed 2026-27 appropriation of $4,275,471 (City budget, p. 372 (https://cao.lacity.gov/content/budget/26-27/2026-27ProposedBudget.pdf#page=372)) is about $1.10 per resident at the City’s 3,898,747 residents in the 2020 Census (LAFD report, citing the Census (https://www.fundlafire.com/s/SOC-Report.pdf)); our calculation. Matching funds actually paid in the 2026 elections were $11.08 million (City Ethics (https://ethics.lacity.gov/cfcs/Display/DisplayPanels.cfc?method=ElectionTotalsResults&useBS4Tabs=yes&showdates=yes&election_id=76)).
California is the only state that bans public financing Yes campaign We did not verify this against an official source.
Who supports and opposes it

California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026 (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)).
Supporters of SB 42 in 2025 included the Los Angeles County Democratic Party, Los Angeles for Democracy Vouchers, Fair Rep LA, Unrig LA, the Green Party of Los Angeles County, the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFSCME and ACLU California Action (Assembly Elections Committee analysis, pp. 7-9 (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2025-06/sb-42-umberg-17513108230298490.pdf#page=7)). ACLU California Action reported spending in support in 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
On the ballot label: California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California and United Latinos Action (ballot label (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/)).
Former FPPC chair Dan Schnur and former commissioner Colleen McAndrews (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Reform California (Carl DeMaio) reported spending against it (Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
The legislators who voted no (SB 42 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42)).
Editorial boards. The Los Angeles Daily News (Sept. 27, 2026 (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/09/27/endorsement-no-on-proposition-4-california-doesnt-need-taxpayer-funded-campaigns/)), San Diego Union-Tribune (Sept. 4, 2026 (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/)) and Santa Rosa Press Democrat (Sept. 18, 2026 (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/18/pd-endorsement-no-on-prop-4-taxpayer-dollars-should-not-support-campaigns/)) editorial boards recommend a no vote. So do the Mercury News and East Bay Times: “Reject Proposition 4” (Mercury News, Oct. 19, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/19/endorsement-reject-prop-4-dont-let-politicians-raid-public-funds-for-their-campaigns/)). So does the San Francisco Chronicle: “We encourage you to vote no again” (SF Chronicle, Oct. 6, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php)). We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026. The California State PTA voted not to take a position (CAPTA (https://capta.org/advocacy/state-ballot-measures/)).

content.thinking:
The polls keep landing with Yes under 50%, so the picture is fairly clear. Most major California editorial boards are opposed, with the Sacramento Bee the main exception. The Yes side has raised only about $757, which is very little.

I'm weighing whether the midterm Democratic enthusiasm and the 42.7% from 2010 suggest a better outcome this time. I'm also checking how similar low-funded legislative measures like 2024's Prop 5 polled against the final result.

Looking back at earlier 2020 and 2018 measures, the polls usually understated the final yes vote a little, though not enough to reach 50%. That leaves the 45% poll for Prop 4 landing somewhere in the mid-40s.

Undecided voters might break mostly against the measure, which would still put the Yes share around 47%. I'm also going to look for other polls, such as internal Yes-side polling or Emerson and SurveyUSA results, to check that estimate.

# Should California taxpayers chip in to fund political campaigns? Prop. 4 lets you decide
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
...
## Effectiveness debate
For now, voters appear skeptical.
