California’s ‘orphaned’ ballot measures
By WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and NICOLE NORMAN (https://www.politico.com/staff/nicole-norman)
10/05/2026 03:09 PM EDT
State Sen. Josh Newman talks during a Senate session in Sacramento, California, on June 11, 2018. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
LEFT BEHIND: Over the last two and a half years, California lawmakers spent countless hours drafting, debating and voting on a group of government reform ballot measures to put before voters. The same energy has not been put toward campaigns to pass them.
Proposition 5, which would change how successors are chosen in recalls, was set for the ballot way back in August 2024. Proposition 4, which would allow for the public financing of campaigns, landed in October 2025. Proposition 2, which would double the amount the state can deposit into its reserves, was rushed to the November ballot earlier this spring.
All aim to reform a somewhat wonky aspect of how government operates, and none of them are easily explainable to voters in a single sentence. And yet each of them have a limited, or non-existent public presence and campaign.
“You get these orphaned initiatives,” said Thad Kousser , a professor of political science at the University of San Diego. “So voters are left with very few bits of information on what’s going to be the most crowded ballot in a decade.”
The recall measure’s travails underscore how quickly a political window can close. In the aftermath of the failed attempt to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom , triumphant Democrats said they were determined to change a system that would allow a challenger — like MAGA tribune Larry Elder (https://www.politico.com/news/2021/08/17/ca-recall-election-larry-elder-505735) — to become governor with fewer votes than the number cast against a recall. Secretary of State Shirley Weber vowed action (https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/09/15/california-elections-chief-wants-recall-overhaul-possibly-as-soon-as-2022-1391082), and election committees revved up (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2021/09/16/with-newsom-secure-democrats-look-to-restrain-recall-494353).
But the momentum soon ebbed. Policymakers couldn’t agree on the changes. Polls showed voters were tepid on changing a process that many see as an important check on elected officials. By the time former State Sen. Josh Newman finally got his measure through, the Newsom recall — and the sense of urgency it engendered — were distant memories.
A spokesperson for the Prop 5 campaign did not reply to requests for comment, although Newman said in a recent interview that he was “not optimistic” about the recall reform measure’s chances.
Historically, the vast majority of measures placed on the ballot by the legislature have won — a full 69% between 1910 and 2025. In the past, that outcome has been largely a function of how many votes it takes for lawmakers to put measures before voters, a two-thirds majority of both houses traditionally meaning that the issue was highly popular.
But polling for the three government reform measures is scattershot. A September Public Policy Institute of California poll had Prop 4 and Prop 5 with only 42% and 35% support, respectively, while Prop 2 had the support of 60% of voters (a later Berkeley IGS poll put Prop 4’s support at 35% for, 35% against, and 30% undecided).
Prop 5 does not appear to have any financial backing or a campaign committee organized to pass the measure. The committee for Prop 4 has a single, $235,000 contribution from Movement Voter PAC, a progressive organizing group. Prop 2’s committee received a $150,000 contribution from Google last week.
Assemblymember Alex Lee , one of the coauthors of the legislation that placed Prop 4 on the ballot, said the measure was in a “good place” and that undecided voters are “ready to be persuaded.” The Prop 4 campaign has begun holding public events and is planning a bus tour at some point this fall.
“I knew the other marquee efforts would absorb the media attention,” Lee said. “Really it’s just about the voter education campaign.”
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , author of Prop 2, said you likely won’t see large ad spends or public appearances to drum up support for expanding the state’s budget reserves. Given the solid polling and what he called the “common sense wisdom” of the measure, he’s confident in its passage.
Meant to shield the state’s budget from the volatility of the stock market, the measure has the support of a wide range of groups, from the California Chamber of Commerce to SEIU. Even so, Gabriel said he expected a “lean campaign” that will “rely a lot on member-to-member communication.”
Each of the government reform measures share at least one key advantage: None face organized opposition.
“Its not like we have to raise X millions of dollars,” Lee said.
Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly , a special Monday edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Questions? Concerns? Tips? Drop ballot measures reporter Will McCarthy a line at [email protected] (https://www.politico.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#65120806060417110d1c25150a090c110c060a4b060a08) .
TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Prop 37: The campaign for a measure to provide loans to help middle-income families purchase homes contributed $300,000 to the California Democratic Party last week, apparently viewing the measure in good financial standing.
2. Prop 38: The No on Prop 38 campaign is operating with a single six-figure check as it tries to run a campaign against billionaire Gary Michelson ’s immunology bond ballot measure. The $3,000 contribution comes from Robert Kaplan , the director of research at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center. Michelson has contributed over $10 million to the initiative, which has come under criticism in recent weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
3. Prop 45: A group of Republican county organizations came out against Prop 45 last week, even as the Yes campaign faced scrutiny for donations (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317427465.html) to Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio ’s Reform California organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730). The Yes campaign, meanwhile, released a report (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) showing what it says would be the “significant economic benefits” of Prop 45, including adding 20,000 homes a year.
4. Fund scientific research (2028): Newsom climbed the Golden Gate Bridge (https://x.com/CAgovernor/status/2105470383281598682) with State Sen. Scott Wiener and a camera crew to sign a $7.5 billion research bond that aims to combat federal funding cuts. The measure will be on the ballot in 2028. “I’m proud to sign a bond to invest in the future of the state of California,” Newsom said in a video from the bridge.
5. Prop 40: Heavily outspent and facing enormous establishment resistance, the wealth tax campaign is hoping America’s most prominent progressive can carry it to victory. Sen. Bernie Sanders is rallying for Prop 40 in Los Angeles today after swinging through San Francisco on Saturday, where he described the campaign as a Democrat-defining battle over “the most important ballot initiative in the country.” (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/03/bernie-sanders-billionaire-tax-san-francisco-rally-01105995)
6. Prop 39: DeMaio is continuing on his “Barbecue, Beer, & Ballots” tour through California, attending his tenth barbecue of the last week in Ramona (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/events/barbeque-beer-ballots-ramona-10-05-2026) today as the campaign looks to help pass Prop 39. As Will wrote for POLITICO Magazine last week (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?utm_source=firefox-newtab-en-us), DeMaio’s grassroots army has become a major factor in his rise in state politics.
7. Measure ER (Los Angeles County): A one-half cent sales tax narrowly approved by Los Angeles County voters in June took effect on Oct. 1. But it could be a while before the $1 billion it is expected to generate each year for health care can actually be spent. A lawsuit, brought by the Libertarian Party of LA County, will have to play out in LA County Superior Court before the proceeds can be used.
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK — Californians for Voting Rights, one of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39, is launching a pair of advertisements in the Bay Area hammering on the “consequences voters will face” should the measure pass. In the first spot, the No campaign characterizes Prop 39 as a “MAGA power grab” led by President Donald Trump (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM). The second warns people (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EbT1lgt8ic4) of longer lines in order to vote. The seven-figure buy is the committee’s first time on air.
IN OTHER NEWS
HE’S BACK: Former Gov. Jerry Brown will tonight join journalist Miriam Pawel , the author of nonfiction works about the Brown family (https://miriampawel.com/the-browns-of-california/) and Cesar Chavez (https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/27/books/review/the-crusades-of-cesar-chavez-by-miriam-pawel.html), for a conversation launching her latest book: “California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California.” The discussion will “explore the history of the University of California, its relationship with California’s political and social life, and the continuing importance of public higher education,” and the event will run from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the California State Library. The retired Brown’s appearance is his latest since he visited the state Capitol during end-of-session proceedings and penned a call for global nuclear (https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/10/08/i-taste-ashes-in-the-wind-nuclear-weapons-jerry-brown/) disarmament. Register here (https://libraryca.libcal.com/event/17654368) .
THE BOOGEYMAN: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC is flooding the airwaves with ads hitting Republicans on Jeffrey Epstein, the late financier and convicted sex offender. They have data to back it up, POLITICO’s Andrew Howard reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/05/democrats-smp-attack-ads-epstein-01106408).
Internal polling of over 4,500 voters from Senate Majority PAC, conducted by the Democratic firm Blue Rose Research late last week and shared with POLITICO, found that a 44% plurality of voters — including the same percentage of swing voters — think the Epstein issue is “serious” and that Republicans should be held responsible.
And while nothing trumps affordability as the issue du jour on the campaign trail this fall, state-level research from SMP found that the Epstein ads can shift races three to six points in Democrats’ direction.

The wealth tax is losing support
By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy)
09/21/2026 03:20 PM EDT
Despite support from progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders, the wealth tax faces an uphill battle. | Jae C. Hong/AP
WEALTH TAX WARNING: A proposed tax on billionaires is faltering in California, according to a new poll by POLITICO and its partners, with public support dropping off as opponents launch a massive advertising blitz.
Fewer than half of likely voters (45%) said they would vote for the tax on the assets of California’s wealthiest residents, while 43% said they would vote against it and 12% were undecided, according to the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a0-c50d-d2df-a1f4-f7cf0f4d0000). That’s down from February, when proponents of the measure, Proposition 40, held an edge (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/10/wealth-tax-leads-in-california-poll-but-faces-major-headwinds-00819733).
“The trend in Prop 40 is certainly going against Prop 40,” said Jack Citrin , a University of California, Berkeley, political science professor and co-director of the poll. “From a historical point of view, you’d think the no side are gaining and would potentially win.”
The proposed one-time, 5% tax has consumed California politics, drawing in Gov. Gavin Newsom and some of the state’s most powerful interest groups. A resounding 83% of likely voters said they had heard some or a great deal about the measure — a remarkably high number given that the main opposition committee only launched its first ad in late August. Likely voters who said they’d heard a “great deal” were opposed by a 57-38 margin.
“The campaign is just starting, and roughly a gazillion dollars are going to be spent on it,” said Jon Cohen , founder and CEO of TrueDot, whose firm fielded the poll. “The fact that the people who are the most tuned in are the most opposed points to significant vulnerability that I think the yes side has.”
Proponents face an overwhelming financial disadvantage. Virtually all of their funding has come from a single health care union, SEIU-UHW, while billionaire foes have allocated tens of millions to beat back and pass rival initiatives that would invalidate Prop 40.
That money will help opponents hammer at messages that look likely to resonate: The Citrin poll found voters were less likely to support Prop 40 if they didn’t believe it would be a one-time tax, as promised. Opponents went on air last week with an ad warning that “when the money runs out, Sacramento will be back with yet another tax.” And while Prop 40 supporters have dismissed that prediction as untrue, they are likely to be drowned out by detractors.
Despite those headwinds, the poll finds a window of opportunity for supporters. The sliver of likely voters who remain undecided are markedly more likely to lean toward voting yes (65%) than no (15%); the initiative is popular with Democratic likely voters, 66% of whom support it; and likely voters across parties are wary of billionaires, with 44% saying they do more harm than good versus 34% who view them favorably.
Still, it is a narrow path. Cohen said “overwhelmingly, the measure’s vulnerability shows in relatively soft support,” and Citrin noted the most persuadable bloc was likely moderate voters who are more receptive to economic warnings and less inclined to an aggressive soak-the-rich message.
“If you think about where the movement would be, it would be presumably not among the strong Democrats or the more liberal Democrats, but from people near the center and independents where the no’s have an opportunity to gain by hammering away at the weaknesses of the measure,” Citrin said.
Regardless of how Prop 40 fares, the poll suggests Newsom’s vehement opposition could be a liability if he seeks the Democratic nomination for president in 2028. A plurality of registered voters — including a plurality of Democrats — were more likely to say Newsom was fighting the tax to “protect billionaires and other wealthy interests” rather than to “protect California’s economy and tax base.”
“This looks more like an issue-specific credibility problem than a broader political collapse,” Cohen said, “but becoming the face of the opposition puts him conspicuously at odds with a sizable share of his coalition.”

TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Prop 39: A new Prop 39 campaign ad (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DH0pY3paoz8&source_ve_path=OTY3MTQ&embeds_referring_euri=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.reformcalifornia.org%2F) aims to distance the ballot measure from Donald Trump , explicitly arguing that the initiative is “completely different from Trump’s proposal” and that you can “dislike Donald Trump and still vote yes on Prop 39.”
2. Prop 3: So far, the fallout from the Prop 40 debate does not appear to have negatively impacted Prop 3, an extension of an existing tax on high earners. PPIC polling released last week showed the measure with 58% support.
3. Prop 44: SEIU-UHW has not contributed any money since May to its effort to impose spending requirements on health clinics, as all its efforts and financial resources are diverted to passing the wealth tax. Last week, the clinics sued SEIU-UHW and its leader Dave Regan (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/09/clinics-file-rico-suit-against-dave-regan-uhw-01084065?site=pro&prod=alert&prodname=alertmail&linktype=headline&source=email) over accusations of extortion and coercion related to the measure, accusations Regan denied.
4. Fund public transit (Bay Area, 2026): The campaign to pass a regional sales tax to fund BART and other transit systems held a “day of action” last week, holding events at stations across the Bay Area and warning of “catastrophic” reductions of services should the measure fail.
5. Prop 2: Largely lost in the shuffle of a high-spending slate of ballot measures is Prop 2, a measure to strengthen the state’s rainy day fund. Six weeks before the election, the measure has little public presence, although a spokesperson said the campaign was “ramping up.” It may not matter. Polling from the Public Policy Institute of California released last week showed majority support for the measure across “age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.”
6. Prop 4: A separate government reform measure appears to be in a more tenuous position. Prop 4, which would allow the public financing of elections in California, had the support of only 42% of likely voters in the same poll. The campaign held a kickoff event in Orange County over the weekend.
7. Data centers referendum (Santa Cruz): County supervisors shot down a proposal (https://pajaronian.com/supervisors-reject-proposal-to-give-voters-say-over-ai-data-centers/) that would have given voters the right to determine whether data centers should be built in unincorporated parts of the county, as voters in California increasingly (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/04/california-ballot-measure-ban-data-centers-monterey-park-00949648) ask for a say in the process.
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK — COALITION BUILDING: The campaign to defeat Prop 43 is touting its growing support from unions, as labor groups organize to defeat a measure that would raise the threshold for local governments to pass new taxes.
The slate of unions include groups representing the state’s teachers, nurses, firefighters and building trades, among other interests. In a release, David Green , an executive board member of SEIU California, said the measure “protects corporate interests at the expense of hardworking Californians.”
“When communities vote to fund their own fire departments, schools, and hospitals, that’s democracy working,” Green said.
SEIU contributed $1 million (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3197031&amendid=0) to the effort opposing Prop 43 late last week.
IN OTHER NEWS
STRIKE A DEAL: Paramount Skydance and the states that sued (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/13/california-tests-its-antitrust-muscle-in-hollywood-00995805) to block the company’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery are poised to settle the antitrust litigation, clearing the way for the blockbuster transaction to close, a person familiar with the negotiation confirmed to POLITICO.
As POLITICO’s Daniel Miller reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/21/paramount-states-to-settle-antitrust-litigation-01086145), the settlement, first reported by Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-21/paramount-to-settle-lawsuits-paving-way-for-warner-bros-merger?itm_source=record&itm_campaign=Paramount&itm_content=Merger_Settlement-0), ends a fractious two-month legal battle that was seen as a major test of California’s ability to exert regulatory power over a high-profile business deal that Trump signaled he wanted completed (https://www.wsj.com/business/media/trump-says-cnn-should-be-sold-as-part-of-any-megadeal-6ca8051a) — and a defining moment for California Attorney General Rob Bonta, whose national profile had risen during the dispute.
AI REGULATION: Rep. Valerie Foushee (D-N.C.) and Del. James Moylan (R-Guam) are preparing to introduce a bill aimed at combating online fraud, including scams powered by artificial intelligence, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp reports. (https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/09/21/congress/ai-powered-online-scams-targeted-in-bipartisan-bill-01086095)
The bill, named Stopping Abuse and Fraud Enabled by Platforms Act, or SAFE Platforms Act, and shared first with POLITICO, is an attempt to combat the growing number of increasingly sophisticated online scams — many powered by AI — that target vulnerable users such as elderly people.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

# Here’s what every proposition on the California ballot is about
### Prop. 4: Public fundraising
State legislators put Proposition 4 on the ballot, asking voters to allow state and local governments to establish public campaign funds for candidates.
If passed, it would reverse a 1988 ban against the practice.
Limits would be in place to ensure funds are not taken from education, transportation or public safety programs.
If passed, the proposition is estimated to cost the state a few hundred thousands of dollars annually for the Fair Political Practices Commission to oversee.
Supporters argue that California is the only state that does not allow for public funding of campaigns, which they say is a way to negate the influence of private money in politics.
Opponents say the proposition will allow politicians to use taxpayer money to fund their campaigns with little limits.
Proposition 4 is endorsed by the California Democratic Party and League of Women Voters, and opposed by the California Taxpayers Association and United Latinos Action.

Still no results, with the election a day away, so I have to make a prediction. I'm weighing whether the 2026 midterm enthusiasm gap among Democrats could mean an electorate more Democratic than the polls assume, though PPIC's likely-voter screen may already account for some of that. I'm also starting to look at Prop 4's ballot position.

I'm checking the Prop 4 ballot label, which says it repeals a ban on public funding of campaigns, and I suspect many low-information voters will balk at that wording. The Yes side spent under $1 million, so its reach is limited. Among Democrats, PPIC shows only 60% support, which isn't overwhelming given the party endorsement, and I'm trying to recall how Prop 15 polled in 2010 before it got 42.7%.

I'm recalling how recent California ballot measures have fared against their final polls. Measures polling in the mid-to-high 40s with few undecideds have usually failed, though Prop 19 in 2020 passed narrowly despite weak polling, and measures without funded opposition sometimes pass anyway.

I'm recalling how past California measures with no funded opposition still failed, like Prop 6 in 2024, which got about 46.7% despite having no organized opponent. So the lack of opposition money doesn't guarantee passage. I'm also noting that several 2020 and 2022 measures split on results that didn't track their polling cleanly.

I'm settling on "no" as the answer, since the evidence points to the measure failing. Before finalizing, I want to check the Whittier 360 article and any other forecasts, plus any late news about spending.

I'm checking the Yes campaign's late spending, which tallies under $1 million across committees, a small amount for a California measure. I'm also planning to confirm the PPIC Prop 4 crosstab numbers, though I already have them, and I'll look at the Whittier 360 article and CalMatters' last-minute guide before deciding.

Whittier 360 predicts six California propositions will pass, six will fail; two remain too close to call
Rebecca Canales (https://www.whittier360newsnetwork.com/profile/f8c940d8-e5eb-46fd-8a58-6834773d6406/profile)
5 minutes ago
5 min read
ELECTION FORECAST
Caption: Whittier 360 News Network forecasts six California propositions will pass and six will fail in the November 3, 2026 election, with two too close to call. AI-generated editorial illustration; predictions are not election results.
Whittier 360 News Network predicts that California voters will approve six statewide propositions and reject six others in the November 3 election. Two additional measures remain too close to call.
These predictions are part of an experimental forecasting approach that Whittier 360 is testing. After the election, we will compare our forecasts with certified results to assess their accuracy.
The predictions below are not endorsements or recommendations on how to vote. A forecast of passage does not indicate our support for a measure, and a forecast of defeat does not indicate our opposition.
Here are our predictions for all 14 statewide propositions, presented in numerical order, with explanations of what each would do if approved.
Proposition 1 — Housing affordability bonds
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for affordable housing programs. Funding would support rental housing, veterans’ mortgages, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable homes and down-payment assistance.
The state estimates repayment costs of approximately $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years.
Proposition 2 — State budget reserves
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 2 would change California’s rules for building its rainy day fund and making additional payments toward state debts. The changes would increase state budget reserves and continue extra debt payments for a longer period.
The reserve fund helps the state manage economic downturns and fluctuations in revenue.
Proposition 3 — Permanent extension of higher income taxes
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 3 would make permanent an existing income tax increase on high-income earners that otherwise expires in 2031. The official summary identifies an individual income threshold above $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation.
The measure would preserve an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue by continuing those tax rates, with revenues allocated to public education.
Proposition 4 — Public financing of election campaigns
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 4 would repeal the prohibition that prevents the state and most local governments from establishing publicly funded campaign programs.
It would allow qualifying programs rather than automatically provide public money to every candidate. Programs would face restrictions on eligible recipients and spending, and could not use money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety.
Proposition 5 — Changes to recall elections
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 5 would change how vacancies are filled after successful recalls. Voters would no longer choose a replacement candidate on the same ballot used to decide whether to remove an official.
Instead, vacancies would generally be filled through a later special election or an appointment, depending on the office and timing. The measure would preserve the ability to recall officials while changing the replacement process.
Proposition 37 — Homebuying assistance
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 37 would create a homebuying assistance program financed through up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. Eligible buyers could obtain fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of the purchase price of qualifying newly constructed homes priced below approximately $1.5 million.
Buyers would have to meet income and residency requirements, occupy the home and contribute at least a 3% down payment. Homeowners’ loan payments would repay the bonds.
Proposition 38 — Medical research bonds
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half would go to a University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and half to research grants.
Estimated repayment costs are $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years. Revenue generated by the research could offset some or all of those costs, but that outcome is not guaranteed.
Proposition 39 — Additional voter identification requirements
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 39 would require government-issued identification for in-person voting. Mail voters would have to place the last four digits of their designated government-issued identification number on their ballot envelope, matching their registration information.
The measure also would require citizenship-verification efforts, annual reporting and free state-issued voter identification cards upon request. Estimated implementation costs range from tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually.
Proposition 40 — One-time billionaire wealth tax
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time tax equal to 5% of the wealth of covered taxpayers with assets exceeding $1 billion. Revenue would primarily support health care.
The state estimates a temporary revenue increase totaling tens of billions of dollars over several years, alongside a possible ongoing reduction in income tax revenue from billionaires.
Proposition 41 — Tax audits and state spending limits
Whittier 360 forecast: TOO CLOSE TO CALL
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exclude their revenues from California’s constitutional spending limit. It also would require pre-election reviews of programs slated to receive funding from voter-proposed special taxes and recurring audits of programs supported by new special taxes.
The proposal could affect other tax measures on the same ballot through provisions addressing conflicting measures. Whittier 360 is withholding a pass-or-fail prediction.
Proposition 42 — Restrictions on new property and retroactive taxes
Whittier 360 prediction: PASS
Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on ownership of personal property, including financial assets and business interests. Personal property in this context means property other than real estate.
It also would restrict certain retroactive taxes and apply to new taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026. The measure contains provisions addressing conflicts with other propositions approved on the same ballot.
Proposition 43 — Higher approval threshold for local special taxes
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 43 would require two-thirds voter approval for voter-proposed local special taxes, replacing the current simple-majority threshold for those measures beginning January 1, 2027.
Special taxes raise money for specified purposes. The change could make it harder to approve certain local funding proposals and could reduce future growth in local tax revenue.
Proposition 44 — Community health clinic spending requirements
Whittier 360 prediction: FAIL
Proposition 44 would require certain nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on qualifying program services advancing their charitable purpose.
Covered clinics failing to meet the requirement could face penalties. The proposal would create new state oversight responsibilities, with administrative costs funded through fees.
Proposition 45 — Environmental review changes
Whittier 360 forecast: TOO CLOSE TO CALL
Proposition 45 would change California Environmental Quality Act procedures for qualifying projects, including many housing, transportation, water and health projects.
It would tighten deadlines for environmental review and court challenges and limit the scope of certain judicial reviews. Whittier 360 is withholding a pass-or-fail prediction because we consider the outcome too uncertain to call.
How the forecast will be evaluated
Our forecast contains six predictions of passage, six predictions of defeat and two uncalled contests. “Too close to call” means we are not predicting a winner; it does not mean we expect an exact tie.
We will assess the 12 pass-or-fail predictions against certified election results and report how many proved correct. The two uncalled measures will be identified separately rather than counted as successful predictions.
Voters will determine the outcomes. These forecasts represent Whittier 360’s assessment before the results are known.
